At Tiangong Monastery in Luoyang was National Teacher Shenxiu, posthumously titled Datong.

He stood eight chi tall, with elegant eyebrows and large ears, possessing the dignified bearing of a high official. Having long heard that the Way at Huangmei was preeminent, he went there to visit and sat together in silent communion.

After the final wailing for the deceased, a great assembly was held at Longhua Temple, where eight thousand monastics and laypeople were fed and fourteen monks were ordained. Two years later, at the second anniversary of his passing, the funeral rites were completed at Ximing Monastery.
As in previous assemblies, the Dharma Master Wanhui (Fayun) requested alms for the inner palace; he personally presented rare and precious items to accompany the offerings.
Lord Zhang Yue (Yan Gong) returned the courtesy of a teacher to his disciple. His disciples Pujì and Yifú were both held in high esteem by both the court and the common people.
As depicted in the Guifeng Chenggong tu (The Diagram of Guifeng Chenggong): "The transformative influence of Puji became increasingly flourishing, and he had thirty dharma heirs.
Among them were Nan Yue Lanzan, Songshan Yixing, Zhongnan Weizheng, and Sanfeng Daoshu—all of whom were unfathomable as to whether they were ordinary beings or sages.
As for Yifu, when he first visited Datong, Datong spoke with him and remarked: 'Wet earth is close to water; dry wood [is close to fire].'"

It was thus. When he was about to pass away, the Master Fayan Wanhui took Fufu’s hand and instructed him earnestly, saying, "Enter deeply into wondrous enlightenment and extensively deliver all sentient beings;
you must exert yourself in this. Fufu resided at Zhongnan for over twenty years.

One day, amidst the flourishing and intermingled growth of bamboos, cypresses, and orchids, there suddenly appeared an old man whose physical bearing was extraordinary and whose beard and hair were white. Bowing his head, he said, "Your disciple [has come from within]..."
He was a "valley-spirit. I fear that if the Master were to depart elsewhere, this mountain would ultimately be abandoned; therefore, I request you once more to remain until your passing.
Not long after, the monastic community of the capital requested that he reside at the Great Ci'en Monastery in the fifth month of that year.

With a thousand officials and their carriages, and the four classes of followers gathered in throngs, he was again summoned by imperial decree to return to the region of Yi and Luo, much like Puji’s disciple Nan-yueh Lan-ts'an under Emperor De-zong.

He dispatched an imperial edict; when it was presented to the Imperial Messenger, [Wuzhu] had no leisure even to wipe away his tears. Take for example Master Xingyi: his *Tianwen* and *Dayan* were known to all the world.
One day he saw Jizang, offered incense and prostrated himself, then pressed his body close and whispered secretly into his ear. Jizang said, "Right, right."
There was nothing he would not do. When he had thus performed the rites three times, he withdrew into the southern room, closed the door, and extinguished himself.
Jìnglì struck the bell, saying, "Yìxíng has passed away. Upon looking, it was indeed so. Pí Guān, the Governor of Hénán, personally witnessed this event.
Wearing mourning garments and carrying the *cuī* and *dié* headbands, he escorted the funeral procession on foot. Zhongnan Wei Zheng served as an attendant to Emperor Wenzong.

Once, while the imperial cuisine included fresh clams, there was one that would not open when pried apart. The Emperor burned incense and prayed to it; suddenly, it opened to reveal an image of Avalokiteśvara, complete in form and exquisitely beautiful.

The Emperor issued an edict to ask Zheng about this. Zheng cited a scripture, saying: "To those who should be saved by the body of a Bodhisattva, the Bodhisattva appears in the body of a Bodhisattva."
He then preached the Dharma for him. The Emperor said, "The Bodhisattva has already manifested his body, yet we have not heard him preach the Dharma.
Zheng said, "Does Your Majesty consider this matter to be extraordinary? The Emperor said, "It is a rare occurrence; I believe it deeply.

Zheng said, "The Bodhisattva has finished preaching the Dharma for Your Majesty. Moved by Zheng’s words, the Emperor issued an edict ordering the installation of Avalokiteśvara images throughout the empire. (3)
On a mountain path amidst the trees, a mountain deity transformed himself into a wild man. His clothing was plain and simple, and his speech was strange and eccentric.
Beyond his words and laughter, he manifested the forms of the four classes of noble celestial beings (*deva-rishi*). At times he emitted divine light; at other times he produced resonant sounds.
The great assembly could not fathom him. Thus ten years passed in silence, without sound or shadow. He then addressed the multitude, saying: "The mountain deity has performed many varied displays."
These two [stratagems] delude us; they are exhausted by this old monk’s “not hearing and not seeing. My own non-hearing and non-seeing are inexhaustible.
Wansong has fully recorded that under the school of Datong, the masters possessed superior resources and strength.

Guifeng, however, relegated them to the "School of Quieting Delusion and Cultivating the Mind. Furthermore, he said: "In terms of the Dharma, there are two meanings: unchanging and following conditions. In terms of persons..."
There are two gates: sudden awakening and gradual cultivation. When these two meanings are revealed, one knows the ultimate purpose of the entire collection of sūtras and śāstras;
when these two gates are opened, one beholds the tracks and precedents of all worthies and sages. The profound intent of Bodhidharma truly lies herein. As for the analogy of sudden awakening:
suppose a person dreams of being bound by shackles and chains; upon waking, must they still remove those shackles and chains? Therefore, [the Sixth Patriarch said:]...
The Patriarch’s Way: "Originally there is not a single thing; why should one bother to sweep away dust? This was Dongshan’s response.
Those who advocate for gradual cultivation are like ice formed from water; it loses its utility for irrigation and washing. Only when melted by fire and the sun does it return to its full function.

Therefore, regarding the Great Universal Path: "From time to time, diligently wipe it clean; do not allow it to be defiled by dust. If we employ the analogy of a mirror, the Great Mirror is like a mirror—fundamentally luminous and fundamentally pure.

The Great Universal Path is like the grime and darkness that must be polished away. Using the two analogies of ice and a dream: [the former represents the nature of reality, while the latter represents deluded perceptions].

In a dream, awakening does not require cultivation; ice must be melted before it can be used. Furthermore, within the teachings there is the purity of original nature and the purity of freedom from defilement;
there is the wisdom that accords with reality and the wisdom that accords with phenomena; there is understanding through appearances and understanding apart from appearances;
there is true emptiness and wondrous existence; there is the ultimate truth and the conventional truth; and even the principles and facts, the nature and characteristics.

The provisional and the real, the sudden and the gradual, the partial and the perfect, the negation and the illumination, existence and non-existence, and the relations between ruler and minister and father and son—these are clearly assigned to the two schools and can be seen with clarity.
Although this involves emotional understanding, those who possess the eye of discernment must know it. The *Zongjing lu* says:
Those who enter our school must first know that there is something to be known, and only then may they take it up and maintain it. Furthermore, the beginning and the end must correspond;
there must be no deficiency in principle or practice, nor any discrepancy between mind and speech. If one enters the Mirror of the School, both principle and practice are perfected.

According to the judgment of the Mirror of the School, Dajian [Huineng] possessed only one eye, whereas Datong [Shenguang] possessed both eyes, perfectly clear and bright. Why is this? Because Dajian possessed the principle...
Yet there is no practice; this means that from the beginning it is eternally pure, requiring no dust-wiping.

Although Great Penetration has already awakened to this, one must still cultivate the polishing of the mirror until it is bright. Thus it is said: "The correct, though correct, is yet biased; the biased, though biased, is yet round.
Unless one has long studied the school of Dongshan, one cannot be spoken with. Wansong once told people: "Where there are waves, there must be water; but water may sometimes be without waves."
Waves. When the ocean of nature is windless, the waves of the mind naturally subside. There is no sublime gateway for the dual benefit of self and others that transcends this.
Guifeng answered the Prefect Wen Cao’s question, saying: "Although the True Principle is indeed brilliantly penetrating, these afflictions are difficult to eliminate suddenly.
It is like when the wind stops abruptly and the waves temporarily cease; how can the practice of a single body be identical to the functioning of a Buddha? One can only rely on emptiness..."
Take stillness as your own essence; do not identify with the physical body. Take true knowledge as your own mind; do not identify with deluded thoughts.
If deluded thoughts arise, do not follow them at all. Then, at the moment of death, you will naturally be unable to be bound by karma.
Huanglong Haitang answered Minister Han Zonggu’s question, saying: "While it is true that there is no dharma remaining outside the mind, one does not yet know the afflictions."
What is this "habitual tendency" (vāsanā) that you wish to exhaust? If you give rise to such a thought, it will instead become the mistake of mistaking a thief for one's own son.

From the time of the ancient patriarchs until now, all spoken teachings have been medicines prescribed according to the illness. Even if there are afflictions and habitual tendencies, they are treated solely with the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision;
these are all skillful means (upāya-kauśalya) and provisional teachings intended to guide and attract beings. If [you insist on] a fixed...

To claim that there are habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) that can be cured is to assume that there are phenomena existing outside the mind that can be exhausted. This is like the famous metaphor of the "spirit-tortoise dragging its tail along the road":
as one tries to wipe away the tracks, new tracks are produced. This may be called "using the mind to employ the mind," and it reveals that the illness has become even deeper.

If one can clearly realize that there are no phenomena outside the mind and no mind outside phenomena, then since both mind and phenomena are non-existent, whom would one wish to instruct in suddenly exhausting [all traces]?
Juefan’s judgment states: "The two elders were both ancestral masters of the past and present. Their skillful means, applied according to the occasion, possessed their own inherent flavor;

there was originally no superiority or inferiority between them. However, the words with which Guifeng responded precisely matched the intent of Han Gong’s question, and his phrasing did not deviate from the fundamental principle.
When compared with the Esoteric (Mijiao) tradition, Huaitang’s attainment was far more extensive."—Wansong.
The Way. Arriving here, we look back and see that Dajian possessed but a single eye; yet in truth, the entire great earth is this single eye of the śramaṇa.
It is also called the "eye that holds fast heaven and earth," which is continuous and does not leak so much as a hair’s breadth.
It is also named the "Vajra-eye at the crown of the head. Great Penetration’s two eyes are perfectly bright and clear—like sawing through a weightstone, shattering emptiness.
"Similarity to emptiness. Setting aside this great penetration for a moment, Wansong says "blind" regarding the eye of Dajian.
How about that? Xuedou comments: "Since he does not accept it as being an eye, what he brings forward must surely be blind.
Do you see the patriarch’s robe and bowl? If one enters the gate here, they are handed over with both hands—not only at Dayu Ridge."
"One at the head of the ridge cannot be lifted up. Even if a man from the state of Qi were to come, let him take it away slowly and steadily.
Wansong says: "The patriarch’s robe and bowl have been reduced to a hundred fragments. Xuedou says: "Since he did not accept it, this must surely be a blind eye.
Tiantong says: "That which was brought forward must surely be an eye; the one who does not accept it is truly [the one with the eye]."
"Blind! Wansong said. "The eyes of one who is blind are perfectly clear; those with sight see only half.
Were it not for meeting a blind man, it would be difficult to discern the truth. Ultimately, how can this matter be resolved? The mountain is distant and the road long—do not light a fire."
Everyone blows out the lamp and walks in the dark.
